case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Waterloo Region v. C.R.
text:
WARNING

The court hearing this matter directs that the
following notice should be attached to the file:

This
is a case under Part III of the
Child and Family Services Act
and is
subject to subsections 45(8) of the Act.
This
subsection and subsection 85(3) of the
Child and Family Services Act
,

which deals with the consequences of failure to comply with subsection 45(8),
read as follows:

45.—
(8)   No
person shall publish or make public information that has the effect of
identifying a child who is a witness at or a participant in a hearing or the
subject of a proceeding, or the child's parent or foster parent or a member of
the child's family.

85.—
(3)   A person who contravenes subsection 45(8) or 76(11)
(publication of identifying information) or an order of prohibiting publication
made under clause 45(7)(
c
) or subsection 45(9), and a director, officer
or employee of a corporation who authorizes, permits or concurs in such a
contravention by the corporation, is guilty of an offence and on conviction is
liable to a fine of not more than $10,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not
more than three years, or to both.

COURT FILE No.: 08/3268-01

Citation:
Children’s Aid Society of
Waterloo Region v. C.R.
, 2009 ONCJ 786

ONTARIO  COURT
OF  JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

THE CHILDREN’S AID SOCIETY OF THE
REGIONAL MUNICIPALITY OF WATERLOO

Applicant,

—  AND  —

C.R.

C.C.

Respondents

Before Justice M.A. McSorley

Heard on April 14, 2009

Reasons for Judgment released  April 30,
2009

Mr. Morscher...............................................................................................
for the applicant Society

C.R.................................................................................................................................... not
present

C.C.................................................................................................................................... not
present

McSorley J.:

Introduction:

[
1
]

The
matter before the court involved a motion for summary judgment brought by the
applicant society in protection proceedings involving one child C.B.C. born […],
2008.  In it’s motion, the society sought confirmation of the statutory
findings, an order that the child was in need of protection pursuant to s.
37(2) (b-i) and (g) of the
Child and Family Services Act,
an order for
8 months supervision placing the child with his mother, no access for the
father and a restraining order against the father.

[
2
]

The
motion for summary judgment was scheduled at the Trial Management Conference on
February 24, 2009 to be heard on April 14, 2009. Mr. C.C. was in attendance at
the trial management conference although Ms. C.R. was not.  Deadlines for the
filing of material on the motion were set on that date.  The parents had until
April 6, 2009 at 12 p.m. to serve and file any affidavit material.  Neither
parent filed any material on the motion.

[
3
]

Mr.
C.C. made several telephone calls to the assistant trial coordinator and the
judges’ administrative assistants over the Easter weekend.  He left several
messages advising that he would not be present in court on April 14, 2009.  He
directed the assistant trial coordinator to look up a web site on which he had
posted a letter received by him from the Waterloo Regional Police Services. This
letter was attached to an affidavit filed at the hearing of the motion.  The
letter prohibited Mr. C.C. from attending the court houses in Cambridge or Kitchener,
unless:

a)

he was compelled to do so by court order
or summons or subpoena, in which case he was to attend and leave immediately
following the completion of court business;

b)

he was required to attend the court
counter or before a Justice of the Peace for legitimate court business; or

c)

he was required to attend a pre-arranged
meeting with a person who has an office or works out of the buildings listed
above.

[
4
]

Mr.
C.C. took the position that he would not attend the hearing unless given a
guarantee that the CAS or the Waterloo Regional Police Services would not make
false allegations against him.  The letter given to Mr. C.C. was dated March
19, 2009.  It is concerning that Mr. C.C. waited until the Easter weekend to
make telephone calls about his appearance when he knew or should have known
that no staff would be present to receive his calls.  It is also concerning
that having received this letter in mid March, Mr. C.C. waited until the last
moment to express reluctance to attend court without some guarantee.  The order
of February 24, 2009 set the date for the motion for summary judgment.  It
provided filing deadlines for the parents.  That order compelled Mr. C.C.’s
attendance either in person or if he chose through representation by a lawyer
or agent. It further compelled him to attend the court counter to file his
affidavit material. Mr. C.C. had no difficulty in attending court on March 24
th
,
five days after the letter, in order to argue a motion regarding disclosure.
In response to the motion heard on that date, Mr. C.C. served three additional
requests for information on the society.   He was present to argue the motion
and had made no requests regarding the letter of March 19
th
.
Finally, Mr. C.C. could have served and filed material on the motion for
summary judgment.  Even if he had not been present, I would have reviewed all
of the material filed. He chose not to do so, even though the letter of March
19
th
, permitted him to attend the court office to file any material
necessary in his proceedings.

[
5
]

Having
regard to these facts, I found that Mr. C.C.’s messages over the Easter weekend
were made in an attempt to delay these proceedings.  Considering that the
letter allowed him to attend for court dates; allowed him to file material on
the motion;  that he had done so in late March 2009 after receiving the letter;
and that the date for the hearing had been scheduled by order on February 24,
2009 and was known to Mr. C.C., I deemed it appropriate to proceed with the
motion.

[
6
]

Ms. C.R. was also not present at the motion and filed no material.
The society indicated that they did not expect her to appear or argue against
the motion.

Background:

[
7
]

The
mother of the child is C.R..  The father of the child is C.C..  Mr. C.C. is the
father of three other children, M. E.C., born […], 1997, L.C.C.,   born […],
1999 and D.L.C., born […], 2002.  Those children were apprehended from their
father’s care in July 2006 as a result of concerns regarding the father’s
decision making in relation to custody issues and the risk of emotional harm to
the children.  On July 26, 2006 the children were placed with their mother N.G.
under an interim without prejudice supervision order.  During the society’s involvement
with the father, Mr. C.C. was found to be uncooperative, hostile, explosive and
aggressive. The society’s protection application sought a supervision order
with the mother.  That protection application was amended to include a request
for an order that the father have no access to the children and further
requested a restraining order.

[
8
]

That
matter went to trial over a period of several months and lasted 22 days.  The
children were found to be in need of protection pursuant to s. 37(2) (b-i) and
(g) of the
CFSA
and were placed with their mother subject to supervision
for 12 months.  In addition, the father was denied access to the children and restrained
from contacting the mother or children directly or indirectly, and prohibited
from attending within 50 metres of the home address or school of the children. Although
Mr. C.C. appealed this decision, his appeal was dismissed on January 30, 2009
for failing to comply with a court order regarding perfecting his appeal. Reference
to the findings in that trial and the parenting capacity assessment that was
completed for the trial were referred to in the submissions of the society and
to which I will also refer.

[
9
]

On
July 31, 2008 the society received a report from Cambridge
Memorial Hospital as a result of a birth alert sent to the hospital advising that Ms.
C.R. had given birth to a boy on […], 2008.  The hospital staff had no concerns
about the care being provided by Ms. C.R. to the child.  The report further
indicated that Mr. C.C. was at the hospital throughout the birth.  On July 31,
2008 child protection worker Anne Newton outlined the long-standing protection
concerns the society had with Mr. C.C., including his irrational and violent
behaviour at times.  Ms. C.R. knew that Mr. C.C. was involved in a custody
dispute with the society but had not sought out any details.  Ms. C.R.
described Mr. C.C. as being kind and gentle and denied any history of violent
or aggressive behaviour. Ms. C.R. agreed to meet the worker on August 1, 2008.

[
10
]

On August 1, 2008 Ms. C.R. met with the worker
and an intake supervisor.  The protection concerns and risk to her and the
child were outlined.  Although shocked by the information she remained calm and
cooperative and jointly devised a safety plan to ensure her safety and that of
the child. The child was apprehended that day from the mother.  The Waterloo
Regional Police and the intake supervisor assisted the mother in finding a
place of safety that was so designated by the society.

[
11
]

On August 6, 2008 an interim without
prejudice order was made placing the child C.B.C. in the care of his mother
subject to terms of supervision, with no access to the father and further
restraining the father from contacting the mother or child.  Throughout the
summer and early fall the mother continued to be cooperative and follow the
safety plan.  Her care of C.B.C. was appropriate.  However, throughout this
time, Ms. C.R. indicated a desire to get on with her life and reconnect with Mr.
C.C..  She also expressed a desire for Mr. C.C. to have access to C.B.C. but
agreed she would not allow such access until the society approved it. She
continued to believe that she was not in any danger from Mr. C.C..

[
12
]

In October 2008, the interim without
prejudice order was varied on consent to permit contact between Mr. C.C. and Ms.
C.R..  The restraining order with respect to C.B.C. remained in effect.

[
13
]

On December 5, 2008 a risk hearing was
conducted.  At that time, Mr. C.C. and Ms. C.R. were invited to participate in
mediation through the family group decision  making program offered through
Community Justice Initiatives.  Mr. C.C. refused to participate in such a
program indicating that the agency that offered the program was “on the
payroll, just as Dr. Glumac was”.  Dr. Glumac completed the Parenting Capacity
Assessment used in the trial regarding Mr. C.C.’s three older children.

[
14
]

On January 13, 2009 reasons for judgment
were received from the risk hearing. An interim order was made placing C.B.C.
with his mother subject to terms of supervision with no access to Mr. C.C..  I
will refer to those reasons later in this decision.

[
15
]

The matter was then placed on the trial list
at the insistance of Mr. C.C. and a trial management conference was to be
arranged by the trial coordinator. It was at the trial management conference on
January 15, 2009 that the matter was adjourned for a motion for summary
judgment and filing deadlines established.

Issues:

[
16
]

The issue before the court on a motion for
summary judgment is whether or not there is a genuine issue for trial or
whether the evidence is such that the outcome is a foregone conclusion.

Position of the Paries:

[
17
]

The society’s position was that there is no
genuine issue for trial having regard to the fact that the father has made no
changes or participated in any programming or counselling since the parenting
capacity assessment was completed or since the judgment of Hardman J. in
September 2008. The society also argued that Frazer J. at the risk hearing
found that the issues of concern raised both in the parenting capacity
assessment and the judgment in September 2008 continued without any change
being made.  The court was not provided with any position by the parents as
they chose not to file any material on the motion and did not attend on the
hearing date.

The Law
:

[
18
]

Rule 16 of the
Family Law Rules provides that after a respondent has served an Answer or after
the time for serving an Answer has expired, a party may make a motion for
summary judgment for a final order without a trial on all or part of any claim
made in the case.  The evidence on such a motion is generally by way of
affidavit and the person responding to the motion must provide specific facts
showing there is a genuine issue for trial and may not rest on mere allegations
or denials.  Assertions of quite improbable things, when completely unsupported
by any corroborative, documentary or other evidence, are not sufficient to
create genuine issues, see
Evans v. Evans
(2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 1317
(Ont. S.C.J.)
, affirmed
(2000), 2000 CarswellOnt 3161 (Ont. C.A.)
.

[
19
]

Pursuant to rule 16(6) the test for granting
summary judgment is met when the moving party satisfies the court that there is
no genuine issue requiring a trial.  This has been interpreted to mean that
there is no genuine issue of material fact requiring a trial for resolution.
Not every disputed fact or question gives rise to a genuine issue for trial.
The court’s role on such a motion is limited to assessing the threshold issue
of whether a genuine issue exists requiring a trial.

[
20
]

The general principle regarding motions for
summary judgment was set out in the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Attorney
General of
Canada

v. Lameman et.al. and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Alberta and Assembly of
First Nations and Federation of Saskatchewan Indian Nations

2008 SCC 14
, at paragraph
10
:

“The
summary judgment rule serves an important purpose in the civil litigation
system. It prevents claims or defences that have no chance of success from
proceeding to trial. Trying unmeritorious claims imposes a heavey price in
terms of time and cost on the parties to litigation and on the justice system.
It is essential to the proper operation of the justice system and beneficial to
the parties that claims that have no chance of success be weeded out at an
early stage.”

[
21
]

The onus is on the party who seeks summary
judgment to show there is no genuine issue for trial.  In paragraph 11 of the
same judgment, the Court stated that “
each side

must put its best
foot forward with respect to the existence or non-existence of material issues
to be tried.” (
emphasis mine)  Further in that paragraph it was held that
the judge may make inferences of fact based on the undisputed facts before the
court, as long as the inferences are strongly supported by the facts.

[
22
]

In the case of CAS of the Regional Municipality
of Waterloo v. V.L. and A.C.P. dated September 14, 2006 Justice Hambly of the
Ontario Superior Court dealt with an appeal from an order of the Ontario Court
of Justice granting a motion for summary judgment and ordering Crown wardship
without access.  At page 21 Hambly J. discussed the test for summary judgment.
At paragraph 48, he accepted the test set out in
Children’s Aid Society of
the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. R. S.
2000 CanLII 22902 (ON CJ)
,
[2000] O.J. No. 4880

where
it was found that the court had to take a ‘good hard look’ at the evidentiary
record.  The case further stated that the respondent must put “her best foot
forward” in disclosing her case in response to the case for the society and  could
not rest on mere allegations or denials.  The respondent must set out in
affidavits specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.  The
CAS need not meet the test of “clearest of cases” as in a motion for summary
judgment pursuant to Rule 20 of the Rules of Civil Procedure.  Hambly J.
further cited the case of
R.A.  v.

Jewish Family and Child Service,

[2001] O.J. No
47
where it was found that the question of whether there is
a genuine issue for trial must be determined in the context of the overarching
principles set out in s.1 of the
Act
that its primary purpose is to
“promote the best interests, protection and well being of children.”  This must
be done considering the narrow times lines constraining the available
dispositions imposed by the
Act.
He agreed that Rule 16 provides a
remedy to “contain and control a child’s drift in litigation” and is meant to
prevent a child from being held in ‘limbo’ while a dysfunctional parent engages
in uncertain attempts to correct his or her inadequacies.

[
23
]

The law under Rule 16 is clear:  the
applicant has the onus to show there is no genuine issue for trial; the
respondent must put his/her best foot forward and not rest on mere allegations
or denials, but set out in affidavit form specific facts showing a genuine
issue for trial; and where there is no chance of success, a final order should
be made.

Analysis:

[
24
]

Not only did the parents fail to put their
best foot forward, they put no case before the court to consider.  The only
evidence filed on the motion was that filed by the society. That evidence raised
serious concerns about the father and lead the court to conclude that if this
matter went to trial at this time, the order requested by the society would be
granted. I come to that conclusion as a result of reviewing the affidavits of
the workers, the emails sent by the father, the parenting capacity assessment,
the judgment released in September and the reasons for judgment on the risk
hearing.

[
25
]

The parentint capacity assessment with
respect to Mr. C.C.’s older children was completed in July 2007 a year after
they were apprehended from the father’s care, by Dr. Glumac, a psychiatrist
certified by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons and licensed in Ontario.

[
26
]

Although Mr. C.C. was scheduled to meet
with Dr. Glumac in late April and early May 2007 he cancelled both appointments
and was not seen until May 11, 2007.  On May 17, 2007 he arrived at Dr.
Glumac’s office and yelled at him from the hallway and insisted that Dr. Glumac
sign a receipt for a letter.  When Dr. Glumac did not agree to do so, Mr. C.C.
stated:  “I can tell I’m not going to get a fair shake from you. Bring it on.”

[
27
]

Dr. Glumac found that although Mr. C.C.
showed no evidence of brain damage, anxiety symptoms, psychosis, mania,
clincial depression, panic disorder, obsessions, compulsions, phobias, post
traumatic stress disorder or attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, his
demeanour was unnaturally deferential, pandering, emotionally stilted and at
times clearly artificial.  Dr. Glumac’s impressions was that Mr. C.C. was an
emotionally disorganized person with serious personality disturbances.

[
28
]

Dr. Glumac found that the father’s chief
emotional handicap was a complete absence of empathy, and an inability to judge
and respond appropriately to the feelings of others.  He found that Mr. C.C.
was prone to disabling anger (temper tantrums) for which  he is unable to take
responsibility or control.  Sullen withdrawal or fury were the only ways he knews
how to relate with people unless his unrealistic demands were gratified in the
momemt. His lack of emotional control seriously influenced his social
judgment.  He blamed everyone around him for his problems and could not see his
role in this process. Dr. Glumac found Mr. C.C. to be intolerant of frustration
and unable to problem solve.

[
29
]

Dr. Glumac also diagnosed Mr. C.C. with
Narcissistic Personality Disorder and found that Mr. C.C. was gravely
compromised in all areas of parenting.

[
30
]

In his summary, Dr. Glumac stated that Mr.
C.C. had a serious personality disorder that makes it impossible for him to
relate normally to others in a meaningful or personal way.  He stated that Mr.
C.C. had no insight into his own emotional and psychological problems and
believed himself to be the victim of the entire community, thus making him
completely unsuitable for any form of treatment.  Dr. Glumac indicated that Mr.
C.C. had demonstrated himself to be completely negligent, abusive and malicious
with his wife and the staff of CAS.  His use of implied threats was
particularly sinister.  Dr. Glumac found Mr. C.C. to be a pathological liar and
fabricator of false allegations, whose shameless manipulation of his children
to promote false allegations against his wife was outrageous without any
comprehension on his part that he was actively harming those he professed to love.
This was further supported by his out of control behaviour toward others in
front of his children.  Dr. Glumac expressed concern for his safety as well as
the saftey of the mother, children and staff at CAS.  He indicated that Mr.
C.C. was fully capable of believing that if he could not have his children, no
one else would or that those who had taken his children from him should be
punished.

[
31
]

As indicated the protection application
concerning Mr. C.C.’s older children was the subject of a 22 day trial.  In
September 2008, Hardman J. released her reasons for judgment wherein she
ordered a 12 month supervision order placing the children with their mother,
ordered no access to the father and restrained him from all contact with the
mother or children.

[
32
]

In her reasons for judgment, Hardman J.
found that the father’s focus from the beginning had been the wrongdoing of the
society and the injustice wrought against him. Mr. C.C. told the court that he
had availed himself of every avenue to attack the society including complaints
to review boards, professional associations and politicians.  He continued to
argue that he was unfairly blamed for everything and was unable to understand
how damaging it was to the children to be subjected to his need to have them
questioned until they told authorities what he wanted them to say. He refused
to accept any advice on how to handle situations that might impact the
children’s best interests and absolutely would not cooperate with the society
to resolve any of the family issues.

[
33
]

Hardman J. found his behaviour toward the
mother and children to be controlling.  He refused to allow the mother
overnight access even though he continued to use her for child care while he
worked.  He obtained an ex parte order for custody on the grounds that she
would flee with the children if given notice.  Hardman J. found this
unsupported by the amount of time he allowed her to have the children in her
unsupervised care.

[
34
]

Prior to the trial, the father had
supervised access to the children.  He brought appropriate snacks and played
with the children.  The access visists were generally loud as a result of the
physical activities the father engaged in with the children.  The society was
concerned about the conversations the father had with C. and his confrontations
with workers, including knocking on the observation window and shouting.  The
father tried to use his access time to serve papers or to make points with the
workers. Although cautioned by workers, he attempted to create conflict at every
opportunity.  As such Hardman J. found the children were subjected to many
incidents of his loud and abusive behaviour.

[
35
]

Many other examples of inappropriate
behaviour by the father in front of the children were cited by Hardman J.  As a
result of the father’s behaviour, his access was suspended.  Mr. C.C. brought a
motion to have his access reinstated, which was ordered on a specified basis.  Mr.
C.C. became impossible to direct at access.  Hardman J. found that he was
completely unable to focus on what he had to do to ensure that access could
continue in a safe and non-anxious way for the children.  The children became
more and more frustrated with the father’s behaviour.  In December 2006, the
oldest child M. did not wish to attend access any further.  In the fall of
2007, C. no longer wished to attend and finally access to L. was suspended
because he also no longer wished to attend.  At the time of the judgment, the
father had had no access to any of the children for at least a year.

[
36
]

The court was concerned about the father’s
unchanging conduct as during the trial he appered to be obsessed with fighting
the society.  When redirected in his questioning of the Executive Director of
the society, he made a general statement condemning the soceity of brutalizing
the families of this region.  When the court attempted to have the father again
resume his questioning, he instead stated that he had a ‘complete and total
hatred for this man’ repeating ‘complete and total, intense, severe.”  He
acknowledged that no amount of anger management counselling was going to take
away any of his hatred, thus confirming Dr. Glumac’s assessment that no form of
treatment would be of benefit to Mr. C.C..

[
37
]

Hardman J. found that the father had
refused to attend the programming recommended to him; had failed to cooperate
in any way with the society; had been hostile and aggressive in his
interactions with the workers; had repeatedly used extremely profane language
to insult workers; had used racial taunts and disrespected them at every
opportunity.  His manner had been intimidating with everyone including
receptionists, workers, supervisors, access supervisors and the executive
director.  When the society attempted to protect its workers from his barrage
of abuse by setting up a special voicemail procedure, he refused to follow the
protocol.

[
38
]

Hardman J. found the father’s complete lack
of insight into the reasonableness or propriety of his behaviour very
concerning.  Despite the court’s caution he was unable to control his behaviour
and she found as a result, that the father demonstrated no respect for anyone
who disagreed with him.

[
39
]

In her conclusion, Hardman J. found that
rather than being able to assure the court he could now be child focused, he
had done the opposite.  She found that his behaviour to the society and its
employees was completely without excuse and that the vehemence and violence of
the father’s language was extraordinary.  She found it concerning that the
father could not control his behaviour even when he knew how important it was
to do so.  No matter how many times he was cautioned, he was unable to refrain
from subjecting his children to emotionally charged conflict.  He was unable to
understand how his actions affected the children and the family.

[
40
]

The court found there was no issue about
placing the children with the father as they had been doing well in the care of
their mother in a stable home for two years and placement with the father would
require supervision by the society, which given his attitude and severe hatred
of them would be fraught with continuing and escalating confrontation and
conflict.  On the issue of access, Hardman J. found that given the position of
the children and the gap in access, unsupervised access would not be in their
best interests and that the court would expect the father to pressure the
children to say all sorts of things about the mother or the society given that
he was not making his decisions based on their best interests.  With respect to
supervised access she found that such access supervised by the society would be
impossible given the father’s relationship with the society and its workers.
She found that the father was prepared to use vulgar, intimidating and personal
remarks to abuse the workers and that he was physically intimidating to them.
She further found that it was inevitable that the children would be exposed to
conflict if the society were to attempt to supervise access.  In assessing the
possibility of family supervision, she found that the paternal grandmother was not
able to focus on the children’s best interests and evidence presented showed
that she did what the father told her to do. A paternal aunt was not willing to
participate as a supervisor.  Although the father’s brother said he would do
what was necessary to facilitate access, the court was concerned that the uncle
lacked insight into the concerns about the father and that it was inevitable
that conflict would arise because the father was not willing to abide by any
terms of access.  This meant that once again the children would eventually be
subjected to more confrontation and conflict.

[
41
]

In finding that access to the father was not
in the best interests of the children, Hardman J. stated that the father was
unable to comply with any expectation and his anger and desire for vengeance
had not disappeared.  She found the evidence was overwhelming that the father
would not be able to simply enjoy access, but would feel driven to attempt to
change the situation and use his access to the children as an opportunity to
keep on trying to justify his behaviour and take down the society.  She found
that although there was little hope that time or treatment would improve the
situation, the father should seek treatment as directed by a pyschiatrist prior
to the court considering any access, supervised or otherwise.

[
42
]

There were several terms of supervision ,
some of which included the requirement that Mr. C.C. attend and undergo an
assessment with a mental health professional as approved by the society and
follow through with all recommendations; that he attend and successfully
complete individual and/or group counselling for individuals who have
perpetrated acts of domestic violence  to learn about power imbalance, the
abuse of power in relationships and the impact of exposure to adult conflict on
children, at an agency approved by the society and follow through with
treatment recommendations; that  both he and the mother refrain from any form
of verbal or physical abuse or violence toward one another or the children;
that both parents attend parenting/individual or group counselling as approved
by the society; that both parents would sign consents to release information
from service providers; that both parents would cooperate with the society; and
that both parents would meet with a worker as requested.  A review of these
terms and conditions is important because it gives the court information on
which to base the determination of whether any real changes have been made by Mr.
C.C. since early September 2008 that would alleviate concerns related to the
child C.B.C. and thus raise an issue for trial.

[
43
]

At the risk hearing regarding C.B.C., heard
in December and decided by written judgment in January 2009, it was evident
that no changes had been made by Mr. C.C..  Frazer J. referred to many of the
same paragraphs from Justice Hardman’s judgment as set out above.  In paragraph
16 of his judgment, Frazer J. noted that Mr. C.C.’s affidavit evidence filed
after the release of the judgment could only be described as a venomous, angry,
spiteful, abusive, vindictive diatribe.  Frazer J. found that Mr. C.C.
continued to avoid responsibility for any of his own actions and to blame any
and all persons who stand in his way in his determination to get what he
wants.  He found that the material filed on the motion (risk hearing) revealed
that nothing had changed with respect to the father.  He also found that the
mother’s position had changed in that she was now aligning herself with the
father and accepted his position that the society was being arbitrary, bullying
